{{Short description|Fractal shape formed from a line segment}}
[[File:Fractal canopy.svg|thumb|right|200px|Angle=2{{pi}}/11, ratio=0.75]]
[[File:asymmetree.svg|thumb|right|Asymmetric fractal canopy resulting from using different angles for left and right branches]]
[[File:asymme_tree.svg|thumb|right|A more realistic tree resulting from a higher branching factor and curved segments]]
In [[geometry]], a '''fractal canopy''', a type of '''fractal tree''', is one of the easiest-to-create types of [[fractal]]s. Each canopy  is created by splitting a line segment into two smaller segments at the end ('''symmetric binary tree'''), and then splitting the two smaller segments as well, and so on, infinitely.<ref>{{cite news|last=Michael Betty|title=Fractals – Geometry between dimensions|newspaper=[[New Scientist]], Vol. 105, N. 1450|date=4 April 1985|pages=31–35}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last=Benoît B. Mandelbrot|title=The fractal geometry of nature|year=1982 |publisher=W.H. Freeman, 1983|isbn=0716711869|url-access=registration|url=https://archive.org/details/fractalgeometryo00beno}}</ref><ref name="Topics">Bello, Ignacio; Kaul, Anton; and Britton, Jack R. (2013). ''Topics in Contemporary Mathematics'', p.511. Cengage Learning. {{ISBN|9781285528892}}.</ref> Canopies are distinguished by the angle between concurrent adjacent segments and ratio between lengths of successive segments.

A fractal canopy must have the following three properties:<ref>Thiriet, Marc (2013). ''Anatomy and Physiology of the Circulatory and Ventilatory Systems'', p.110. Springer Science & Business Media. {{ISBN|9781461494690}}.</ref>
#The angle between any two neighboring line segments is the same throughout the fractal.
#The ratio of lengths of any two consecutive line segments is constant.
#Points all the way at the end of the smallest line segments are interconnected, which is to say the entire figure is a [[Graph (discrete mathematics)#Connected graph|connected graph]].
The [[pulmonary system]] used by humans to breathe resembles a fractal canopy,<ref name="Topics"/> as do [[tree]]s, [[blood vessel]]s, [[viscous fingering]], [[electrical breakdown]], and [[crystal]]s with appropriately adjusted growth velocity from seed.<ref>Lines, M.E. (1994). ''On the Shoulders of Giants'', p.245. CRC Press. {{ISBN|9780750301039}}.</ref>

==H tree==
{| style="collapse:collapsed;"
| valign="top"|{{main|H tree}}
The [[H tree]] is a [[fractal]] tree structure constructed from [[perpendicular]] [[line segment]]s, each smaller by a factor of the [[square root of 2]] from the next larger adjacent segment. It is so called because its repeating pattern resembles the letter "H".

It has [[Hausdorff dimension]] 2, and comes arbitrarily close to every point in a [[rectangle]]. Its applications include [[VLSI]] design and microwave engineering.{{Clear|left}}
|[[File:H tree.svg|thumb|300px|[[H tree]]: angle={{pi}}, ratio={{math|[[Square root of 2|{{sqrt|2}}]]}}; [[Hausdorff dimension]]: 2]]
|}
